check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self to the mother, confirms the infant's name and age, and handles the infant gently.
Uses plain language, acknowledges the mother's worry and explains what they are doing.
History
Characterises the vomiting:

kids.x: Onset 5 days ago and getting worse, now after almost every feed
Hungry and keen to feed again straight after vomiting

check.x: Asks specifically whether the vomit has been green (bile) or contained blood, and says why green vomit matters (malrotation with volvulus).
Asks about intake and output: feeding pattern, wet nappies (2 in 12 hours) and stools.
Screens for other causes: fever, diarrhoea, cough, rash, jaundice and how alert he has been.
Birth, growth and background: term birth, weight at the 2-week check (4.4 kg), first-born, medicines including any antibiotics, and the father's operation for vomiting as a baby.
Explores the mother's ideas, concerns and expectations, including her worry that she caused it.
Examination
Assesses general state and hydration:

kids.x: Sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, no tears and reduced skin turgor
Weighs him and compares with the previous weight (about 9% loss)

check.x: Assesses circulation: heart rate, central CRT, peripheral temperature, pulses and BP.
Asks for a BGL, as every vomiting infant needs one.
Examines the abdomen with the infant calm: looks for visible peristalsis (ideally during a test feed) and palpates for an olive-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen.
Checks the groins and genitalia for a hernia and looks at the vomit and nappy for bile or blood.
Interpretation
Recognises significant dehydration with compensated shock: HR 170, CRT 3 seconds and cool peripheries with a normal BP, a sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes and about 9% weight loss.

Interprets the gas as a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.52, bicarbonate 36, chloride 88, potassium 3.0) with a normal lactate, and explains it: loss of acid and chloride in the vomit, then the kidney holding sodium at the cost of potassium and hydrogen.
States that the ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis: wall thickness 5 mm and channel length 19 mm.

Considers other causes and what argues against them: malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting), reflux, gastroenteritis, infection such as a UTI or sepsis, raised intracranial pressure, and salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (which gives low sodium, high potassium and an acidosis, the opposite pattern).
Interprets the repeat gas: bicarbonate 26 mmol/L is back to normal and chloride 103 mmol/L is corrected, potassium is normal and he is passing urine, so he is ready for theatre.
Management
Keeps him nil by mouth, inserts an IV cannula and takes bloods for the gas, electrolytes and BGL.
Gives a 0.9% sodium chloride bolus for compensated shock: 10 mL/kg = 40 mL for 4 kg, then reassesses HR and CRT and repeats if still shocked.

Then gives 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit, as the RCH guidelines set out: maintenance 4 mL/kg/h = 16 mL/h plus a 5% deficit (200 mL) over 24 hours, about 8 mL/h, so about 24 mL/h for 4 kg (1.5 times maintenance); adds potassium once he is passing urine; avoids hypotonic fluid.

States that surgery is urgent but not an emergency, and waits until the dehydration and electrolytes are corrected, in particular a normal bicarbonate (many units use bicarbonate below 28 to 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L), with repeat electrolytes and BGL monitoring.
Refers early to the paediatric surgical team for pyloromyotomy and admits him under their care.

Explains pyloric stenosis to the mother in plain language (a thickened muscle at the outlet of the stomach), reassures her it is not caused by her feeding, and explains why he is dry and why the blood tests matter.

Explains the plan: a drip and no feeds for now, an operation once the blood salts are corrected, an excellent outcome, it does not come back, and feeds usually restart within hours of the operation. Checks understanding.
Safety netting
Asks the nurse to call them straight away while he waits for surgery if he vomits green, his heart rate rises or his perfusion worsens again, he becomes harder to wake, or a BGL is low.

Tells the mother to return to the ED after discharge (or call 000 if he is floppy or hard to wake) for repeated forceful or green vomiting, fewer wet nappies, poor feeding or drowsiness, fever, or redness or discharge from the wound.
Arranges follow-up after discharge: a weight and wound check with the GP or maternal and child health nurse within a week, and surgical review as the team arranges.

desc: This station involves a focused history from the mother and an examination of a 5-week-old boy with worsening vomiting after feeds, then interpreting his observations, venous gas and ultrasound, outlining fluid resuscitation and the plan for surgery, and safety-netting the mother.
explain:
Diagnosis

The classic picture is a first-born boy aged 3 to 6 weeks with non-bilious projectile vomiting who stays hungry after vomiting. A family history, especially in a parent, raises the risk. An olive mass or visible peristalsis may be found, and ultrasound confirms the diagnosis (here a wall thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 19 mm). Bilious vomiting needs urgent exclusion of malrotation with volvulus. Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia can also present with vomiting and dehydration in a young boy, but gives hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and an acidosis.

Why the metabolic alkalosis develops

Persistent vomiting of gastric contents loses hydrogen and chloride ions. Volume depletion then stimulates aldosterone, which retains sodium at the cost of potassium and hydrogen excretion. The result is a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with dehydration.

Resuscitation before surgery

Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency but a surgical urgency, not an emergency. Keep the infant nil by mouth and treat shock with a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus (40 mL for 4 kg), then reassess. Then give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit. The RCH Intravenous fluids guideline replaces no more than a 5% deficit over 24 hours on top of maintenance: for 4 kg that is 16 mL/h maintenance plus about 8 mL/h, about 24 mL/h (1.5 times maintenance). Add potassium once the infant is passing urine. Operating before the alkalosis is corrected risks post-anaesthetic apnoea, because the respiratory compensation for the alkalosis (hypoventilation) leaves the infant vulnerable. The RCH guideline waits in particular for a normal bicarbonate; many units use bicarbonate below 28 to 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L as their targets, and the repeat gas here meets them.

Safety netting

While he waits, the nurse should escalate bilious vomiting, worsening perfusion, drowsiness or a low BGL. After pyloromyotomy, feeds restart within hours and the condition does not recur. Parents should return for repeated forceful or green vomiting, fewer wet nappies, poor feeding, fever or a red or discharging wound, with a weight and wound check after discharge.
focus: Pyloric stenosis: a vomiting infant, dehydration and the metabolic alkalosis
guide:
In Part 1, the mother answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. In Part 2, hand over the results and ask the questions in order.

A high-performing candidate takes a focused history that confirms non-bilious projectile vomiting and screens for other causes, checks the BGL, recognises compensated shock with moderate dehydration, interprets the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and the ultrasound, gives a 10 mL/kg bolus (40 mL) and then maintenance plus deficit (about 24 mL/h), explains that surgery waits for a normal bicarbonate and a corrected chloride, and recognises that the repeat gas meets this. Accept "severe" as well as "moderate" for the dehydration if the candidate recognises the shock. They explain the diagnosis and plan without jargon, reassure the mother about the cause and the outcome, and give specific return advice.

A borderline candidate identifies pyloric stenosis but does not ask about bile, misses the BGL, delays fluid resuscitation, does not know that surgery waits for the alkalosis to be corrected or suggests early theatre or oral feeds, and gives vague safety netting.
patient:
Role: You are the mother of a 5-week-old boy who weighs 4.0 kg today. You are worried and tired. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine, and the nurse gives the observations and the BGL if asked. If the candidate asks to watch a test feed, the nurse gives a small feed so they can look at the abdomen.

Opening line: "He keeps throwing up after his feeds, and it shoots right out. He isn't keeping anything down."

History (give only when asked):

  • The vomiting started 5 days ago, a few times a day at first. Now it happens soon after almost every feed.
  • The vomit is forceful and shoots out of his mouth. It looks like milk or curdled milk. It has never been green or yellow, and there has been no blood in it.
  • He is hungry straight after vomiting and wants to feed again.
  • He is breastfed every 2 to 3 hours and feeds keenly.
  • Only 2 wet nappies in the last 12 hours (he usually has 6 or more a day). His poos are small, pasty and fewer than usual. No diarrhoea.
  • No fever, cough, runny nose, rash or yellow skin. He has been sleepier than usual today.
  • He weighed 4.4 kg at his 2-week check with the maternal and child health nurse.
  • Born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal birth with no problems. He is your first baby. He had his hepatitis B vaccine at birth.
  • No medicines, and he has never had antibiotics. No allergies.
  • Family history: his father had an operation for vomiting as a baby. You are not sure what it was called.
  • He lives with you and his father. Nobody at home is unwell.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it might be reflux, or that your milk does not agree with him, and you worry you are doing something wrong with his feeding. You are frightened because he looks thinner. You were hoping for a medicine for reflux.

Questions to ask if there is time: "Did I do something wrong with his feeding?" "Why is he so sleepy?"
points: Pyloric stenosis causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Correct dehydration and electrolytes before surgery; the RCH guideline waits in particular for a normal bicarbonate (many units use bicarbonate below 28 to 30 mmol/L and chloride above 100 mmol/L).
Treat shock with a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, then give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit, adding potassium once the infant is passing urine.
Check the BGL in every vomiting infant and keep the infant nil by mouth.
Bilious vomiting is a surgical emergency and is not pyloric stenosis until proven otherwise.
stem: You are the junior doctor in a paediatric Emergency Department. A 5-week-old boy has been brought in by his mother because he has been vomiting after feeds, and it is getting worse. He weighs 4.0 kg today. A nurse has attached monitoring and is with you.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother and perform a focused examination of the infant, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the infant's observations, a venous blood gas, an ultrasound report and a repeat gas the next day. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, with fluid volumes for this infant, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Projectile vomiting in a 5-week-old infant

part2.lead: Here are his observations from arrival to the next morning, a venous blood gas and the ultrasound report. The last result is a repeat gas the next morning, after 24 hours of IV fluids.

handover.label: Observations from arrival to the next morning
handover.result: Weight 4.0 kg on arrival (4.4 kg at the 2-week check).

rows.note: On arrival: cool hands and feet, sleepy but rousable
Next morning: 5 wet nappies overnight; repeat gas taken

handover.model:
On arrival (08:30): HR 170 is at the top of the RCH acceptable range for a young infant (about 115 to 170), and with a CRT of 3 seconds, cool hands and feet and a sleepy baby who rouses to voice, while BP 85/50 is still normal for his age, this is compensated shock. RR 40 and SpO2 98% in air are normal, he is afebrile, and the BGL of 4.1 mmol/L is normal. With a 0.4 kg (about 9%) weight loss, this is significant dehydration with shock.

Response: after the first bolus HR falls to 152 and CRT to 2 seconds and he is alert, so a second bolus is not needed; he passes urine by 13:30, so potassium can go into the fluids; and by the next morning HR 135, CRT under 2 seconds, 5 wet nappies and a BGL of 5.0 show he is rehydrated. While he waits for theatre, a rising HR, a longer CRT, drowsiness or a low BGL means calling the doctor straight away.

handover.label: Venous blood gas with electrolytes
handover.result: Venous sample, 08:45, at cannulation, before IV fluids.
handover.model:
pH 7.52 is an alkalaemia; bicarbonate 36 and base excess +12.4 make it a metabolic alkalosis, and pCO2 46, in the upper half of the venous range, is the expected partial respiratory compensation (hypoventilation). Chloride 88 and potassium 3.0 are low, sodium 134 is low-normal and lactate 1.2 is normal: a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. It comes from losing acid and chloride in the vomit, then the volume-depleted kidney holding sodium (aldosterone) at the cost of potassium and hydrogen, and it is the opposite of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (low sodium, high potassium, acidosis).

It changes the plan: he must not go to theatre yet, because the compensating hypoventilation risks apnoea after anaesthesia. Resuscitate with 0.9% sodium chloride, then give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose, add potassium once he passes urine, and repeat the gas until the bicarbonate is normal and the chloride corrected.

handover.label: Abdominal ultrasound
handover.result:
Ultrasound abdomen (pylorus), 10:40.

Clinical details: 5-week-old boy, 5 days of worsening non-bilious projectile vomiting, dehydrated. Pyloric stenosis?

Findings:

  • Stomach: distended with fluid and milk, with vigorous peristalsis.
  • Pylorus: muscle wall thickness 5 mm (abnormal 3 mm or more) and pyloric channel length 19 mm (abnormal 15 mm or more). The channel stays closed throughout 10 minutes of scanning and little fluid passes from the full stomach into the duodenum.
  • Mesenteric vessels: the superior mesenteric vein lies to the right of the superior mesenteric artery (normal relationship).
  • Liver, gallbladder and kidneys: normal. No free fluid.

Conclusion: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
handover.model:
The scan confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: a wall thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 19 mm are both above the diagnostic thresholds (3 mm and 15 mm), and the channel stays closed with little gastric emptying. The normal superior mesenteric vessel relationship is reassuring against malrotation, which fits the non-bilious vomiting, though it does not exclude it: green vomiting would still need an urgent contrast study.

The diagnosis is now certain, so he is referred to the paediatric surgeons for pyloromyotomy, but the scan does not make it an emergency operation: surgery waits until the dehydration and the alkalosis are corrected.

handover.label: Repeat venous gas the next morning
handover.result: Venous sample, 08:40 the next morning, after the first fluid bolus and 24 hours of IV fluids.
handover.model:
Against the arrival gas: pH 7.41, bicarbonate 26 and base excess +1.6 are now normal, chloride has risen from 88 to 103 and potassium from 3.0 to 3.9, and sodium, lactate and glucose are normal. With the morning observations (HR 135, CRT under 2 seconds, 5 wet nappies overnight, BGL 5.0), he is rehydrated and the alkalosis is corrected: a bicarbonate below 28 and a chloride above 100 meet the usual pre-operative targets.

He is ready for pyloromyotomy today. Keep him nil by mouth on IV maintenance with potassium until theatre, keep checking the BGL, and tell his mother the operation can go ahead.

ask: You are now calling the paediatric surgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of this 5-week-old boy, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of this baby now, here in the emergency department.
Before he goes home after his operation, what would you tell his mother, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
Identify: self, ED junior doctor; 5-week-old boy, 4.0 kg.

Situation: 5 days of worsening non-bilious projectile vomiting with compensated shock; ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis.

Background: term, first-born, hungry after vomits, 2 wet nappies in 12 hours, father had an operation for vomiting as a baby; 4.4 kg down to 4.0 kg (about 9%).

Assessment:

  • Obs: HR 170, CRT 3 s, cool peripheries, sleepy, BP normal: compensated shock; BGL 4.1 normal; improved after a 10 mL/kg bolus
  • Gas: pH 7.52, HCO3 36, Cl 88, K 3.0, normal lactate: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Ultrasound: wall 5 mm, channel 19 mm: pyloric stenosis
  • Repeat gas: HCO3 26, Cl 103, K 3.9: corrected

Recommendation: admit under paediatric surgery; ready for pyloromyotomy today; please review.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: first-born boy aged 5 weeks; forceful non-bilious vomiting, worsening; hungry straight after vomiting; father had infant surgery; hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; ultrasound wall 5 mm (3 mm or more) and channel 19 mm (15 mm or more).

  • Malrotation with volvulus: must be excluded; against: never green, normal SMV/SMA relationship (does not exclude it)
  • Reflux: against: forceful, worsening, weight loss, shock, alkalosis
  • Gastroenteritis or sepsis/UTI: against: no fever or diarrhoea, nobody unwell at home, normal lactate
  • Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia: against: would give low sodium, high potassium and acidosis, the opposite pattern

1. Nil by mouth, IV cannula, gas, electrolytes and BGL; monitoring.
  2. Compensated shock: 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg = 40 mL, reassess HR and CRT, repeat if still shocked.
  3. Then 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose: maintenance 16 mL/h plus 5% deficit (200 mL over 24 h, about 8 mL/h) = about 24 mL/h; add potassium once passing urine; no hypotonic fluid.
  4. Surgery urgent, not an emergency: wait for rehydration and normal bicarbonate (below 28 to 30) and chloride above 100 (risk of post-anaesthetic apnoea); repeat gas and BGL. Repeat gas (HCO3 26, Cl 103) meets this.
  5. Early referral to paediatric surgery for pyloromyotomy; admit under them.
  6. Nurse to call for green vomit, rising HR or worse perfusion, harder to wake, low BGL.
  7. Explain to mother: thickened stomach-outlet muscle, not her fault, excellent outcome.

What to tell his mother:

  • Feeds usually restart within hours of the operation; it does not come back
  • Come back to the ED for repeated forceful or green vomiting, fewer wet nappies, poor feeding or drowsiness, fever, or redness or discharge from the wound
  • Call 000 if he is floppy or hard to wake
  • Checks her understanding

Follow-up:

  • Weight and wound check with the GP or maternal and child health nurse within a week
  • Surgical review as the team arranges
